chapter_theme: A single song at Vijayapuram (விஜயபுரம்) on the body: a hut of gut, fat and bone with nine gates of filth, quicker to vanish than a water bubble, which the poet desired and tried to keep with medicines and yogas; he asks to reach the anklet-bearing feet; the praise names Siva burning the triple city and Murugan born of his eye.

815.reading: The poet describes the body as gut, fat, bone, flesh, blood and nerves, wrapped in skin so the filth sloshes within, a hut with nine gates of impurity, perishing faster than a bubble on water; desiring this ashen body, he kept trying worthless medicines and many yogas until his anguished mind cried 'enough, enough', and he asks whether he will now reach the beautiful flower feet with anklets. The praise names the night-roamers dead, the mountain crushed, the great sea dried and the gods freed from prison, Siva who bent Meru with the thousand-hooded serpent and burned the triple city with a smile and glared at Kama, and Murugan who came from his eye and grew on the Ganga, at Vijayapuram.
815.nuance: குடல் நிணம் என்பு புலால் ... ஒன்பது வாசலை உடைய குரம்பை: the body is the familiar hut with nine openings. The plea rejects the means of preserving it: சாரமில் அவுடதமும் பல யோகமும் முயலா நின்று அலமரு சிந்தையின் ஆகுலம் அலமலம், medicines and yogas tried on the body are a source of anguish, not rescue.

links.note: Both name the body's nine openings and the filth inside a skin covering: the Naladiyar's fool praises a pot that seeps from nine holes, and 815 calls the body a hut with nine gates, its filth sloshing under the skin.

Tirumular says that if the body perishes the life perishes before knowledge is won, so he learned the means of nurturing the body; 815 calls the same effort, many medicines and yogas tried on a body that bursts quicker than a bubble, an anguish to be given up for the Lord's feet. The tension holds if 815's yogas are read as practices for preserving the body, as the context of அவாவி suggests.
